Switch a function to caller's privilegesalter function public.f(int) security invoker;

False Positives

This lint flags every SECURITY DEFINER function in a user schema with EXECUTE granted to anon. There are two situations where the finding is not a real risk:

  • The function is intentionally a public API endpoint. A "rate-limited contact form" or "anonymous vote" function is meant to be SECURITY DEFINER (so it can write to a table anon cannot otherwise write to) and meant to be executable by anon. Confirm the function validates input and limits what it does, then suppress.
  • The owner is a low-privilege role. If the function's owner has no more privileges than the caller, SECURITY DEFINER does not actually escalate. This is rare because Supabase functions are typically owned by a privileged role, but worth checking the owner column shown above.

In every other case the lint is reporting a real privilege escalation: a caller with the public anon key can run code that reads or writes data they otherwise could not.

Level: WARN

Summary: This SECURITY DEFINER function is callable by signed-in users.

Ramification: Because this function is SECURITY DEFINER, it runs with the privileges of its owner rather than the caller. If authenticated has EXECUTE, any signed-in user can call it through POST /rest/v1/rpc/<name> and potentially read or modify data that RLS would normally block. In projects with open signup, that can mean any throwaway account, so revoke EXECUTE, switch the function to SECURITY INVOKER, or move it out of your exposed API schema if every account holder should not be able to call it.

See also: lint 0028_anon_security_definer_function_executable. The two checks are paired — revoking from one role alone usually leaves the other side callable. Address findings from both lints together. The pg_graphql_* lints (0026/0027) cover the parallel risk for tables/views.

So calling the function returns rows that the caller — authenticated — could never read with a direct SELECT.

PostgREST exposes it at /rest/v1/rpc/<name> automatically; pg_graphql exposes it as a query or mutation field if the return type is supported. They can still be problematic if the underlying tables are unprotected, but that risk is covered by lints 0008_rls_enabled_no_policy and 0013_rls_disabled_in_public on the data, not by this lint on the function.

How to Resolve

The fix is per-function. For each finding, decide whether authenticated should genuinely be able to invoke the operation, then take one of three paths:

Option 1: Revoke EXECUTE (most common)

1
revoke execute on function public.my_priv_op(int, text) from authenticated, anon, public;

Revoke from PUBLIC as well, because Postgres' default-grant lives there. Revoking from anon at the same time also clears the matching 0028 finding.

1

Suitable when the function does not actually need to bypass RLS — it was just declared SECURITY DEFINER by habit or default.

Option 3: Keep both SECURITY DEFINER and the EXECUTE grant — intentional

Identifying the Owner

To see who the function actually runs as (this is what determines what RLS it bypasses):

1
select
2
    p.proname,
3

5

Quick Reference

GoalSQL

False Positives

This lint flags every SECURITY DEFINER function in a user schema with EXECUTE granted to authenticated. There are two situations where the finding is not a real risk:

  • The function is intentionally a per-user privileged operation. A "register my account profile" or "submit feedback as me" function may be SECURITY DEFINER (so it can write to a table authenticated cannot otherwise write to) and meant to be executable by every signed-up user. Confirm the function validates input and limits what it does, then suppress.
  • The owner is a low-privilege role. If the function's owner has no more privileges than the caller, SECURITY DEFINER does not actually escalate. This is rare because Supabase functions are typically owned by a privileged role, but worth checking the owner column shown above.

In every other case the lint is reporting a real privilege escalation: any signed-up user — including throwaway accounts created via open signup — can run code that reads or writes data they otherwise could not.

Level: INFO

Summary: Detects tables where autovacuum_enabled=false has been set as a storage parameter.

Ramification: Dead tuples accumulate without bound, causing table bloat that degrades query performance and increases storage costs. The effect compounds after any UPDATE or DELETE workload.

Rationale

PostgreSQL autovacuum reclaims space from dead tuples left by UPDATE and DELETE operations. Disabling it at the table level (ALTER TABLE t SET (autovacuum_enabled = false)) prevents this cleanup entirely for that table, regardless of the cluster-level autovacuum setting.

How to Resolve

Re-enable autovacuum and reclaim existing dead tuples immediately:

1
ALTER TABLE public.orders RESET (autovacuum_enabled);
2
VACUUM ANALYZE public.orders;

False Positives

This lint may fire when the setting is intentional:

  • Read-only archive tables — no UPDATEs or DELETEs means no dead tuples; autovacuum has nothing to do.
  • Bulk-load staging tables — autovacuum is temporarily disabled to avoid I/O contention during ETL; should be re-enabled after the load completes.
  • Manual vacuum schedules — tables vacuumed explicitly via pg_cron or another scheduler; autovacuum is disabled to avoid conflicts with the scheduled job.

In these cases the lint can be safely ignored, but verify the table is not accumulating dead tuples via pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup.

Level: ERROR / WARN

Summary: This function is callable without signing in and appears to EXECUTE a SQL string passed in by the caller.

Ramification: The function is reachable through POST /rest/v1/rpc/<name>, so anyone with the public anon key can run arbitrary SQL through it. If the function is SECURITY DEFINER the SQL runs as the function owner and bypasses RLS. If it is SECURITY INVOKER the SQL runs as anon and is limited by that role's grants and RLS. The level is ERROR for a SECURITY DEFINER function whose parameter appears directly in an EXECUTE, and WARN for everything else, including SECURITY INVOKER functions and functions matched only because a parameter has a SQL-like name. Either way the caller can read your schema and any data anon can reach. Revoke EXECUTE, or replace the function with fixed operations.

See also: lint 0032_authenticated_dynamic_sql_function_executable. It is the same check for signed-in users. Revoking from anon alone usually leaves the function callable by every signed-up user, so address both together. Lint 0028_anon_security_definer_function_executable covers SECURITY DEFINER functions exposed to anon in general.

Rationale

Helpers like exec_sql(query text) or run_query(sql text) let a client send SQL to the database and get the result back. Postgres grants EXECUTE on new functions to PUBLIC, and Supabase also grants it to anon and authenticated, so a function like this is callable by clients unless EXECUTE is revoked. Checking that the string starts with select does not make it safe.

This lint reads the function body, and only for PL/pgSQL functions in exposed schemas. A function is flagged when:

  1. a text or varchar parameter (or an array of either, including VARIADIC) is used inside an EXECUTE statement, or
  2. a text or varchar parameter (or an array of either, including VARIADIC) is named like SQL (sql, query, stmt, statement, command, cmd, ...) and the body contains an EXECUTE anywhere.

Parameters bound with EXECUTE ... USING and parameters wrapped in quote_ident(), quote_literal() or quote_nullable() are not counted.

How to Resolve

Option 1: Revoke EXECUTE

1
revoke execute on function public.exec_sql(text) from anon, public;

Option 2: Drop the function

1
drop function public.exec_sql(text);

Option 3: Replace it with fixed operations

Expose one function per operation with typed arguments and no string-built SQL. If you have to build SQL, pass values with EXECUTE ... USING, quote identifiers with quote_ident(), and check table and column names against an allow-list.

Example

Given this function:

1
create function public.exec_sql(query text) returns json
2
language plpgsql security definer as $$
3
declare r json;
4
begin
5
  execute 'select json_agg(t) from (' || query || ') t' into r;
6
  return r;
7
end $$;

Fix:

1
revoke execute on function public.exec_sql(text) from anon, authenticated, public;

False Positives

  • A text parameter used as an identifier through format('%I', param) is safe but can still be flagged. Use quote_ident(param) instead.
  • A function that checks the string against a strict allow-list before running it. Confirm the allow-list is complete, then suppress the finding.
  • Only PL/pgSQL bodies are inspected. Functions in other languages, or that build SQL in a helper function, are not detected.

Level: ERROR / WARN

Summary: This function is callable by signed-in users and appears to EXECUTE a SQL string passed in by the caller.

Ramification: The function is reachable through POST /rest/v1/rpc/<name>, so any signed-in user (with open signup, anyone with a throwaway account) can run arbitrary SQL through it. If the function is SECURITY DEFINER the SQL runs as the function owner and bypasses RLS. If it is SECURITY INVOKER the SQL runs as authenticated and is limited by that role's grants and RLS. The level is ERROR for a SECURITY DEFINER function whose parameter appears directly in an EXECUTE, and WARN for everything else, including SECURITY INVOKER functions and functions matched only because a parameter has a SQL-like name. Either way the caller can read your schema and any data authenticated can reach. Revoke EXECUTE, or replace the function with fixed operations.

See also: lint 0031_anon_dynamic_sql_function_executable. It is the same check for anon. Revoking from authenticated alone can leave the function callable without signing in, so address both together. Lint 0029_authenticated_security_definer_function_executable covers SECURITY DEFINER functions exposed to authenticated in general.

Rationale

Helpers like exec_sql(query text) or run_query(sql text) let a client send SQL to the database and get the result back. Postgres grants EXECUTE on new functions to PUBLIC, and Supabase also grants it to anon and authenticated, so a function like this is callable by clients unless EXECUTE is revoked. Checking that the string starts with select does not make it safe.

This lint reads the function body, and only for PL/pgSQL functions in exposed schemas. A function is flagged when:

  1. a text or varchar parameter (or an array of either, including VARIADIC) is used inside an EXECUTE statement, or
  2. a text or varchar parameter (or an array of either, including VARIADIC) is named like SQL (sql, query, stmt, statement, command, cmd, ...) and the body contains an EXECUTE anywhere.

Parameters bound with EXECUTE ... USING and parameters wrapped in quote_ident(), quote_literal() or quote_nullable() are not counted.

How to Resolve

Option 1: Revoke EXECUTE

1
revoke execute on function public.exec_sql(text) from authenticated, public;

Option 2: Drop the function

1
drop function public.exec_sql(text);

Option 3: Replace it with fixed operations

Expose one function per operation with typed arguments and no string-built SQL. If you have to build SQL, pass values with EXECUTE ... USING, quote identifiers with quote_ident(), and check table and column names against an allow-list.

Example

Given this function:

1
create function public.exec_sql(query text) returns json
2
language plpgsql security definer as $$
3
declare r json;
4
begin
5
  execute 'select json_agg(t) from (' || query || ') t' into r;
6
  return r;
7
end $$;

Fix:

1
revoke execute on function public.exec_sql(text) from anon, authenticated, public;

False Positives

  • A text parameter used as an identifier through format('%I', param) is safe but can still be flagged. Use quote_ident(param) instead.
  • A function that checks the string against a strict allow-list before running it. Confirm the allow-list is complete, then suppress the finding.
  • Only PL/pgSQL bodies are inspected. Functions in other languages, or that build SQL in a helper function, are not detected.
